stimulus.text:
“That we being chiefly of the African extract, and by reason of long bondage and hard slavery, we have been deprived of enjoying the profits of our labor or the advantage of inheriting estates from our parents, as our neighbors the white people do. . . . Your petitioners further show, that we apprehend ourselves to be aggrieved, in that, while we are not allowed the privilege of freemen of the State, having no vote or influence in the election of those that tax us, yet many of our colour (as is well known) have cheerfully entered the field of battle in the defence of the common cause. . . .”
— Petition of Paul Cuffe, John Cuffe, and five others to the Massachusetts General Court, February 10, 1780 (abridged)

stem: The petition's argument mattered after 1780 mainly because its language

options.text: Was language the Massachusetts constitution and courts then applied to Black residents
Convinced the legislature to grant the petitioners' request at once
options.misconception: The legislature denied the petition; the men got no relief from taxation when they asked for it.

options.text: Ended slavery in Massachusetts in the year the petition was filed
options.misconception: Slavery ended through court decisions in 1781-1783, not through this petition in 1780.

options.text: Persuaded southern states to adopt gradual emancipation laws
options.misconception: No southern state adopted gradual emancipation; the petition's effect ran through Massachusetts law, not the South.

rationales.A: The petition spoke of freemen's privileges and taxation without representation. Background: the 1780 constitution set voting by property, not race, and court decisions in 1781-1783 ended slavery in Massachusetts.
rationales.B: The petition was denied when filed; its power came later, as its language entered the constitution and the courts.
rationales.C: 1780 is too early: the court cases that ended Massachusetts slavery came in 1781-1783, after the petition.
rationales.D: The South never followed; the petition's language mattered in Massachusetts, where the constitution and courts took it up.
rationales.general:
1. Note the denial. The legislature gave the petitioners no relief in 1780.
2. Follow the language. Background: freemen's privileges and representation reappear in the 1780 constitution.
3. Follow it to court. Background: Massachusetts court decisions of 1781-1783 read the constitution's equality as ending slavery.
Remember: a denied petition can still win — ask where its words show up next, not only whether it was granted.
